rows.label: Share of a tobacco-control policy's long-run cut in smoking that comes in its first years (smokers quitting)
rows.explainer: Lyle and Hendrie (Globalization and Health, 2024, Methods) take the long-term effect of a policy, the change in prevalence after 40 years, as the first-year effect times a multiplier: 2 for taxes and warnings, 1.25 for smoke-free laws, 1.3 for marketing bans, 2.5 for cessation. So about half of the long-run cut (40% to 80%: one over the multipliers) comes at once, from smokers who quit; the rest builds over decades from young people who never start. For taxes, smoke-free, flavour and marketing rules; a law that only stops young people starting (the UK's smokefree generation) is all never-start.

rows.label: Years from a smoker quitting until the health gain
rows.explainer: Quitters cut their heart-disease risk within a few years and their cancer and lung-disease risk over 5 to 20 (Doll et al., BMJ 2004: stopping at 30 avoids almost all of smoking's excess deaths, at 50 about half); the burden a quitter averts comes on average about 8 years later. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years from a young person kept from starting to smoke until the health gain
rows.explainer: People start smoking at 14 to 25 and smoking kills and disables mostly at 50 to 80: 69% of the UK's smoking deaths, 58% of the US's and 44% in the ten countries are at 70 or older (facts: death_ages), so a young person kept from starting gains mostly four to six decades later, the illness part (chronic lung disease) a little sooner. The UK's impact assessment of its smokefree-generation law finds "no health benefits would be expected until 2044" (para. 178), 17 years after the law starts, with gains rising to 2100. 40 years, 30 to 50. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Tobacco control: delay from a won tax or law to its start
rows.explainer: Taxes take effect at once or at the next budget year; regulations and bans within months to two years (Indonesia's 2024 regulation phases in; Vietnam's e-cigarette ban took effect in January 2025). 1 year, 0.25 to 2.

rows.label: Share of US smoking DALYs a typical year's US tobacco-control wins (by all groups) avert once in full effect
rows.explainer: A year's US wins by everyone working on them: one or two state tax rises (Indiana's $2 a pack in 2025), local flavour bans (Denver's, upheld by voters in November 2024), Tobacco 21 and e-cigarette enforcement and court wins (FDA v. Wages and White Lion, April 2025), against setbacks (the FDA's menthol ban withdrawn in January 2025). Worked out: a $1 rise on an $8 pack cuts cigarette consumption about 5% (price elasticity about -0.4), and the number of smokers about half as much, 2.5% (about half the response is quitting, half smoking less; the burden follows smokers); one or two states' rises cover a few percent of Americans, about 0.1% fewer smokers nationally; flavour and youth rules (fewer young people starting) about 1.5 times as much again. 0.25%, 0.08% to 0.7%. A long-run fall in smoking, so it reads as a share of the smoking burden in the steady state. Each charity's share of the credit is its own model's.

rows.label: US tobacco-control wins: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: Only the validity of the effect sizes (unmeasured outcomes are the missing-data discount, leakage the enforcement figure): price elasticities and flavour-restriction studies are well established in the US; the step from fewer smokers to less burden in the steady state is less sure. 0.8, 0.5 to 1.

rows.label: US tobacco-control wins: share enforced as written
rows.explainer: US taxes are collected and age and flavour rules mostly enforced; illegal disposable e-cigarettes and cross-border buying leak some of the effect. 0.9, 0.75 to 1.

rows.label: Harm of vaping as a share of the harm of smoking, per person
rows.explainer: Public Health England's 2015 review put vaping at "around 95% safer" than smoking, and the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities' 2022 update found exposure to toxicants far lower in people who only vape; the US National Academies (2018) found substantial evidence that switching completely cuts exposure, but long-term harms (heart and lung) are not yet observed. 10%, 3% to 33%, above the 5% for the unknowns. Read where a policy moves people between smoking and vaping.

rows.label: UK Tobacco and Vapes Act: share of a covered cohort kept from smoking
rows.explainer: The impact assessment's central scenario (a 30% fall in the yearly rate of taking up smoking below the age of sale, picked with tobacco-control experts (19 consulted, 14 replied) and chosen over stronger scenarios to allow for underage sales and proxy purchases, paras 154-161) takes smoking among 14 to 30 year olds from 9.2% in the baseline to effectively zero, "9.2 percentage points lower in 2056" (para. 169). That is the high end. Our best guess, 8 points, takes a little off for a baseline already falling faster than the assessment's flat steady state (a criticism made to the Public Bill Committee); leakage is not taken off again. The low end, 2.5 points, is the assessment's weakest scenario (Scenario 5, 6.7% against 9.2%, Table 27). The November 2024 assessment for the reintroduced bill keeps the same smokefree-generation modelling.

rows.label: Lifetime DALYs lost per person in the UK who smokes as a young adult

source.title: Doll, Peto, Boreham and Sutherland, Mortality in relation to smoking: 50 years' observations on male British doctors, BMJ 2004

rows.explainer: Lifelong smokers die about 10 years sooner (Doll et al.), and stopping at 30 avoids almost all of that, at 40 most of it. Many young smokers stop, so a person smoking at 14 to 30 loses a few healthy years on average, deaths and illness from heart disease, cancer and lung disease together. Check against the impact assessment: a covered UK cohort gains about 198,000 DALYs undiscounted (824,000 × 8% × 3), about 109,000 at the government's 1.5% over 40 years; the assessment's own figure, deaths only and only those before 2100, is about 950,000 QALYs in present value (£66.7bn at £70,000) over all the cohorts it covers, most of whose smoking deaths fall after 2100, so roughly nine cohorts' worth by our figure. Consistent within the range.

rows.label: UK Tobacco and Vapes Act: share of all the campaigning behind it done in the year to 31 March 2026
rows.explainer: The law is won (Royal Assent April 2026, three weeks after the year ends), so the question is how much of the win this year's work bought. The bill was introduced in November 2024 and spent this year in the House of Lords, the last stretch of a campaign that ran from the 2023 plan (and of decades of tobacco-control work before it). A fifth, from about four years of active campaigning with the final year weighing more. Read by every model of a charity whose year ends on 31 March 2026 (Cancer Research UK, the British Heart Foundation).

rows.label: UK Tobacco and Vapes Act: delay from the year to March 2026 to the sale ban's start
rows.explainer: The sale ban starts on 1 January 2027 (the impact assessment's appraisal starts on that date), about a year after the middle of the year to March 2026. The longer wait until the health gains is never_start_lag_years.

rows.label: UK Tobacco and Vapes Act: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The effect of a generational sale ban is modelled, not observed (New Zealand repealed its own before it took effect), and a later government could repeal it; underage sales and leakage are already in the assessment's central scenario and uk_act_prevalence_cut, and switching to vaping is its own side effect (uk_act_vaping_substitution_share). So 0.7, as medical research's evidence adjustment, is for modelling risk and repeal alone.

rows.label: UK Tobacco and Vapes Act: campaigning groups' share of everyone's resources behind it
rows.explainer: The government proposed and drafted the law and Parliament passed it (ministers' and civil servants' time counts among the resources, Convention 2); the rest is the campaigning groups: Action on Smoking and Health, Cancer Research UK, the British Heart Foundation, the royal colleges, the British Medical Association, directors of public health. 40%, 25% to 60%. Each charity's model credits it its own share of this (adv_share_of_campaigners), so the charities' credits together stay within it.

rows.label: UK Tobacco and Vapes Act: share of the young people it keeps from smoking who vape regularly instead
rows.explainer: Vapes stay on sale to adults (the same Act restricts their flavours, packaging and display), and among 16 to 24 year olds in Great Britain more vape than smoke (ONS, Adult smoking habits in the UK: 2023). Many would-be smokers already vape as well, so only the extra vaping counts. 30%, 10% to 60%; × vaping_relative_harm it is a harm, a side effect of the smoking averted.
